In the chilling underbelly of a secluded bunker, Donald's life was snuffed out by deadly snake venom and now, it's up to the sharp and relentless Detective Winston to shake the truth out of his prime suspects, Jay and Autumn.

I was inside the local café, mulling over the case when I saw Autumn. She was a regular here, always engrossed in a murder mystery novel, which somehow comforted me in a way. Detective work made you appreciate the mundane things about life.

"Autumn," I greeted her as I approached, "how are things?" 

She took a moment, reached down into her bag, and pulled out a specific thrilling novel titled "Perfect Crime". She glanced up from the book and responded, "Oh, hello Winston. Just the usual."

I looked down at her book, the title striking a chord, "This one any good?"

Autumn got excited and spoke in vivid detail about the perfect crime plotted in the novel. Her enthusiasm around the theme of crime and the specific details almost perturbed me, but I chose to focus on the dialogue at hand.

We mentioned Donald, and how he had plans⟦ to⟧ head to the bunker. Autumn froze for a moment before returning to her normal composure. "He trusted you," I said, "would have let you in the bunker."

"The bunker? Yeah, I know the place. Donald used to talk about it," she replied, trying to sound nonchalant. But I could discern a hint of unease in her voice, the knowledge of the bunker and everything that had transpired there appeared to weigh heavy on her.

Autumn had been in a gang with Donald. Back in the day, they used to own this town, running around and kicking up dust wherever they went. Time moved on, things had changed, but the past lingered in Autumn's fear of her past crimes revealing themselves.

Donald had confided in me once that he discovered Autumn was still engaging in criminal activities. She had psychic abilities which made her an asset in their criminal past and perhaps, in her current endeavours.

The clang of the door brought me back to the café. Autumn had left, the sunshine reflected off her hair as she headed down the street, her murder mystery novel tucked securely under her arm. The people in the café moved again, life resumed while questions circled in my mind. Along with Autumn, I left the café: one looking to uphold justice, and the other, potentially, to evade it.

Winston walked down the long, subterranean corridor again, guiding his flashlight along the intricately detailed blueprints of the bunker he held in his hands - blueprints that once belonged to the experienced Jay. Once housed in the station, this giant underground maze was a known territory to Jay, of course, but to Winston, it was all foreign.

Hours later, in a makeshift interrogation center in the surface barracks, Winston eyed the familiar face of the missionary, Jay.

"I've seen the blueprints, Jay," he said simply, watching the other man's face.

"Oh, those?" Jay replied, a light airiness showing in his reply. "I spent quite a bit of time down there when I was stationed at this bunker. I could still walk through it blindfolded."

"And isolated…" Winston added, his gaze never leaving Jay's face. It was a known fact that the underground bunker locked from the inside and the only two keys existed – one with Donald and the other with Jay. It had been established earlier that Jay and Donald were the only ones inside the fortified bunker during the time of Donald's death.

Jay didn't respond immediately. He looked disinterested, detached. He finally spoke up, "I guess Donald had started to suspect, huh? He confronted me about it a few days ago."

"You've done some snake handling, haven't you?" - Winston asked.

Jay chuckled. "A rite of passage, they call it. Over there in the region with a high snake population, it’s a trial, a blessing, an exorcism.” His tone held a grim, respectful distance. 

Winston nodded, "I've heard it's common among missionaries to learn about snakebite remedies as well."

"A living antidote, in case of a bite, that's not common knowledge."- Jay answered, leaning back in his chair.

"Were you aware, Jay," Winston began, "that Donald discovered certain… irregularities?"

Jay's eyes flickered to Winston's for the first time. "Irregularities? You mean the smuggling?" He admitted.

Winston let the confession hang in the air between them.

"I was using the missions to distribute certain substances, that part is true." Jay said.

"You got trained here, in the bunker. Now you distribute substances, in religious ruse. " His tone turned pointedly menacing. 

He leaned in slightly, resting his elbows on the tabletop, "Discovery of which, Jay, would do a lot more than tarnish a reputation."

Jay remained silent, his eyes hardening and body rigid, awaiting the impending threat the detective presented. 

Winston suddenly backed off, taking his notes and exiting the room, leaving Jay alone among his thoughts.<turn|>

In the quiet solitude of a local library, Philip is found shockingly murdered with a barbed wire, leaving Detective Winston with the arduous task of sifting truth from alibis of the two main suspects, Hugo and Maria.

Winston's mind was buzzing during the ride to the local hair salon, a tragic incident sinking his spirits. Philip, a library frequenter, was dead, with dire circumstances suggesting a gruesome murder. The weapon, a coil of barbed wire, unusual for sure. As he walked into the salon, he saw a middle-aged woman, Maria with a multitude of barbed hairpins reflecting ominously under the lights. She was working away with a pair of scissors, her nimble fingers managing both the razor and the various hairpins with the dexterity of an artist.

"Maria?" Winston asked.

Caught off guard, Maria looked up, her eyes wide in surprise. "Yes, detective, can I help you with something?" she answered, never pausing her delicate dance of grooming. She clicked her scissors, moved on to her razor, then her infamous collection of barbed hairpins, all with the practiced ease of someone in her profession for a long time. 

"I hear you've been doing this for over fifteen years?" he asked, partially making small talk, partially feeling out the woman in front of him.

"Sixteen years, next Tuesday." She replied, her gaze deliberately focused on her current client's head. 

"Quite a long time..." Winston said, thoughtful. "You ever do hair for a fellow called Philip?"

Maria paused for a moment, her eyes downcast. "Yes, I did his hair once. He's the one found in the library, right?"

"Yes," Winston nodded, "I heard about your usual evening strolls to the library. The one open late till 10 pm?"

"Yeah, it's quiet, peaceful. They don't mind if I bring my coffee inside. I even have a key, just in case I lose track of time and it's closing," Maria disclosed.

"I see. How about Robert? Phillip's fiance. He been here, recently?" Winston changed the subject.

Maria swallowed and cleared her throat, stepping away from her customer to face Winston. "Yes, he came... to talk." 

"To talk about the wedding, or about that time in high school where you confessed your love to him before he proposed to Philip?" Winston probed.

Maria averted her eyes, "About the wedding... but, yes, we also brought up the past. I've been in love with Robert since high school, and I've been secretly carrying that love for years, you know."

Winston observed Maria. Things certainly aren't always as they seem, he thought, as she returned to her client, her barbed hairpins dancing in the slightly unsettling light. The fact that the time of Philip's death aligned eerily with Maria's usual library visit was an added layer of unease. "Well, Robert's supposed to marry Philip soon, isn't he?" 

"Yes, but things aren't always as they seem, detective." Maria's voice held an edge as she responded, her gaze being both hurt yet defiant, hinting at a deeper tale yet to unravel.

Blowing off steam, jumping from coffee shop to coffee shop, Winston was back on track, unanswered questions regarding Philip's mysterious murder bouncing in his mind. Known for his capacity for violence to get what he wanted, Philip had a reputation; ironically, barbed wire, his common form of conflict resolution, had been the weapon.

The detectives at the precinct were all a twitter about the eccentric sound technician, Hugo. Out of all potential suspects they'd drawn in, one thing about Hugo was blinking on Winston's radar. Not once had any colleague, friend or customer ever been invited to his personal studio where Hugo spent most of his time. The man was protective of his private space, it seemed. 

"I'm detouring to Hugo's office," Winston informed his partner as he made a left turn.

The professional layout of Hugo's studio stood testament to his skills. Winston noticed the different⟦ categories⟧ of wires neatly stowed away, labeled by type. Spools of common wires were neatly packed, then his gaze floated towards an unusual collection of unique wires, barbed wire included, labeled 'personal collection'. He stroked one with his gloved fingers, lost in thought.

"Hugo," Winston called for his attention, "This is some impressive collection. Not everyone works with barbed wire in a sound system, huh?" Hugo's smile was gentle, "I just like to keep my wire knowledge versatile," he shrugged.

"I heard you missed out on this year's industry conference," Winston inquired casually. 

"Yeah. Conferences are not my cup of tea," Hugo chuckled, "Too much show and too little know. I prefer focusing on the actual job, here in my studio."

Casual chat moved reflective as Winston asked about Philip, "What about Philip? Ever get into a formal tussle with him?" Hugo's rifle through a box of cables paused, "No direct confrontation, sir, but I was an unfortunate audience to threats he made to my brother over a phone call. Nastiest conversation ever."

Winston nodded, taking in the distraught sound engineer before himself. Hugo's brother owed a significant amount to Philip, everyone and their nephew knew that. It had been no blind gamble, but rather a bet gone awry. It had complicated Hugo's personal dynamics, certainly. Especially so since no one saw Hugo at the annual company holiday party. Usually a regular, Hugo's absence sent alerts.

Duty kept Hugo traveling between different venues for sound gigs, with a vast array of tools tagging all along, wires included, also, wires very similar to the ones found at Philip's crime scene. Winston mulled over this kaleidoscope of details, knowing well the devil lay in their details, as he drove back to the precinct.<turn|>

Winston rolled his shoulders, trying to ease out the stiffness from his long drive up the mountain. Here he was at a vibrant chalet, which was recently the scene of a horrifying event. Evelyn, a well-known tarot reader in the town, and a frequent visitor at Malaysia's place for years, greeted him. Oddly, she was known to always bring Malaysia's spare set of chalet keys with her on each visit. "Ah, Detective Winston, so good of you to finally join us," she noted with bitterness.

"I see you've made yourself at home, Evelyn," Winston nodded towards her open suitcases, purposely ignoring her remark.

"It's been transferred to my name after...after Malaysia's..." Evelyn's lips trembled, the melancholy in her eyes genuine.

"Well, your card was drawn, I suppose." Winston hinted, "Always wanted a chalet of your own?"

Evelyn returned his glance sharply, "I won't deny that. But that doesn't mean I'd do anything drastic." Evelyn, a decades-old hunter initially drawn to the chalet's by the lure of game larger than even a human being, stated defensively. Her love for hunting and the thrill of pursuing such large game were known to all too well in town.

"Hmm. I'm surprised your extensive hunting experiences didn’t convince you to get one sooner. You've really been at it for years, haven't you?"

A small smile emerged on Evelyn's face, "Ah, yes. Hunting is my...passion. Love the thrill of hunting animals of all sizes."

"I'm sure. The gun shop just⟦ down⟧ the street told me you recently bought a new rifle that peculiarly matches the description of the murder weapon," stated Winston, trying to mask suspicion from his tone.

A flicker of surprise registered on Evelyn's face, "Well, yes. I had just bought a new one recently. But...but..."

Winston took a mental note of her surprise, before standing, "Thanks for your time, Evelyn. Your name on the gun shop records has been enlightening. I'll see myself out."

Evelyn appeared taken aback, "Oh...um...if you need anything else...you know where to find me." 

As Winston sauntered back to his car, he recognized that his next task would be to double-check the gun shop's records and reclaim the security footage that links Evelyn’s purchasing transaction. He was on the brink of substantiating some valuable information.

Winston toiled through the heat, questioning people, pulling at strings. The chalet incident was a head-scratcher– it wasn’t often that he saw such crimes, especially not with a rifle.

"Letti," he said moving to the window, "you said you were home the night of the murder, right?"

"Yeah," Letti answered, not meeting his eyes.

"But you confirmed you stayed at the chalet the night before the murder, and a staff member even recognized your car parked there overnight." There was no immediate response. His eyes darted back to the notes.

“Minutes ago, I spoke to one of your friends who came here with you," he said, his gaze unwavering as he maintained eye contact with her. “She testified that you seemed unusually angered by Malaysia's new relationship."

"Can't see what that has to do with anything," Letti retorted, shrugging her shoulders.

He recalled a recent public event where Letti was a known presence. There had been controversy swirling around racist comments she had made – it had even made the local news. He brought it up, “And at that public event last month, you’ve made quite a spectacle with your racist comments."

And then there was the incident at the chalet. He was getting word of it now, "And what about the chaos you caused at the chalet just before Malaysia was killed? Your actions there were described as terrorist-like." Winston's brow furrowed. His mind spiraling further into the investigation.

While he dealt with her in person, Winston thought back to the results of his earlier investigation, combing through Letti's open social media account. He found what he expected– consistent derogatory comments, racial slurs, and toxic language.

He looked back up from his screen. “During one of those parties, we caught you having a conversation with a known criminal. One of our officers overheard you two discussing illegal activities."

In conclusion, he pointed out one last damning piece of evidence. “Let’s not forget your frequent visits to a bar whose owner has been convicted for illegal alcohol trading.”

A web of uncertainty was weaving itself, linking Letti to a nexus of unsavory activities. He knew he had to keep a closer eye on her, and hoped that she wouldn’t make any rash moves until he could piece it all together. Time was ticking away. He ended the conversation with no further comment from Letti, silently vowing to not let Malaysia’s death go unsolved.<turn|>

After another tiring day of working the case, Winston parked his car in a quiet, dimly lit street outside of a popular local gym. Inside was Sophie, his latest person of interest, who had gained notoriety for expressing racist viewpoints at several social gatherings. Witnesses and victims had come forth, stating that Sophie, in her fury, had confronted and threatened individuals belonging to the groups she so openly expressed prejudice against.

Sophie, who was known for her athletic prowess as a professional trident thrower, was amid an intense workout when Winston entered the facility. She was preparing for an upcoming competition, her muscles rippling under the strain of each precise throw. Her unlimited access to the gym's professional equipment made this process much easier.

Winston approached her once she finished her practice throws. "Ms. Sophie," he greeted, his gaze unwavering.

She turned, her eyes blazing with a competitive energy. "Detective Winston," she replied. "Can I help you?"

"Maybe. I'm asking around about a gym guest, Stephen. He was part of your clientele, wasn't he?" He knew the answer, having found that Stephen visited this gym regularly.

Sophie's expression hardened. "Yes," she confirmed. "So what?"

"Stephen has been murdered in the library downtown." Winston noticed Sophie's eyes flicker with surprise, or guilt perhaps. Sophie knew Stephen's routine well. His unusual, long hours spent at the library coincided with the time of the crime, a detail Sophie was well aware of. 

Sophie looked genuinely shocked. "Library?" she echoed, her brows furrowing.

"Yes, the library. Quite an unusual scene, isn't it? Especially when we found a trident near his body. It happens to be identical to the kind here in your gym," Winston added.

Immediately, Sophie blanched. She swiveled her head towards the impressive array of trident equipment, nervously mimicking a laugh. “A trident?” she repeated, “Yes… we do have tridents here for… for our clients.”

Winston changed his line of questioning. "Stephen belonged to a particular minority group, didn't he? One I've heard which you've openly threatened and discriminated against at several social events. Isn't that so?"

Sophie, visibly taken aback, struggled to reply, "I...I have...expressed my views at some social gatherings," she stammered out, her face reddening. "But what's that got to do with Stephen?"

"Well, knowing when Stephen would be at the library," Winston began, "and considering your skill with tridents, the weapon implicated in the crime – I just thought it could be worth looking into."

With those parting words, Winston left the bewildered Sophie in silence inside the gym. This first encounter provided him with more than enough to investigate Sophie further.

In the wake of a gruesome flamethrower murder at a local soccer field, seasoned detective Winston steps up to investigate, with suspects Sophia and Larry under his watchful eye.


"Detective Winston," Sophia greeted as she shuffled her cardboard coffee cup in her hands nervously. They were standing on the edge of the football field where the murder had taken place.

"Sophia," Winston nodded, looking out at the half-time huddle of sweaty, tired players - the same scene where Savannah had taken her last breath. 

Sophia was a journalist. She'd been covering the match when Savannah was killed, following her usual line of reportage. Today, she'd been on the field, right where it all happened. Savannah's murder had occurred right at halftime and yet, nobody seemed to know anything. 

"So, it's been a while since your reports on the military exhibition, correct?" Winston asked, keeping his face calm but watchful to catch any change in her expression.

"Yeah,  it was a couple of months ago. I still have the flamethrower I'd managed to keep, for research and, you know... reminders," Sophia said, her gaze flickering toward the field. 

Winston nodded. He knew that keeping memorabilia wasn't uncommon in her trade. Did it provide Sophia with a flamethrower when she needed one?

"Savannah, were you two friends?" Winston asked, keeping an eye on the middle of the field where everything had happened.

In the serene isolation of a snow-draped chalet, Harry's life is abruptly ended by the vicious snap of a bear trap; now, it's up to the astute Detective Winston to unravel the deadly web spun by the questionable duo, Dexter and Gordon.

Winston was sitting in his car, gazing at the misty country road that led to Gordon's farm. Bad news was often paired with a country farm, but today was particularly grave - A death at the chalet, a bear trap, and a farmer named Gordon.

Winston slowly climbed out of the car as he neared the farmhouse - a large wooden structure isolated in the distant country land, adjacent to a somber cemetery.⟦ The⟧ only cemetery in town, he thought. Isolated, just like Gordon, its only neighbor who immigrated here with no known family. Gordon had landed there, growing crops, breeding animals, keeping up a farm.

He walked up the pathway onto the farm, noticing the creaking wooden sign that read 'Gordon's Hunting Supplies'. It was evident that Gordon was more than just a standard farmer. The sign was riddled with buckshot. 'Bear problems,' Winston thought to himself as he made his way to the front door. 

Gordon was sitting on a rickety wooden stool as Winston made his approach. He was weathered from years of outdoor work and his eyes carried an unmistakable lonesome pain. His fists were gripped around a wooden handle, tapping rhythmically onto the dry farm soil. He was tense.

"Gordon?" Winston quietly asked. The man nodded in response keeping his gaze fixed intently on the horizons towards the cemetery. 

Having heard about Gordon's regular evening walks towards the cemetery, Winston tried to carefully navigate the conversation towards Harry. 

"Heard you folks had quite a fuss at the farmer's market recently?" The old farmer barely reacted, still lost in his world. 

"Took away your best customer, did he?" added Winston, trying to draw Gordon out. He was referring to the fact that their recent altercation was born out of Harry winning an award for his agricultural products - a feat that Gordon declared was a result of favoritism and had led to his sales dropping.

Minutes of silence passed before Gordon finally spoke haltingly, "Harry cost me my sales, my livelihood... Those people chose his products over mine."

Then, as if realizing he'd said too much, Gordon hastily added, "But that's all he took. I got no hard feelings.”

Winston carefully listened but made no attempt to comfort Gordon or press the matter further. He took one final look at the brooding farmer, jotting down the conversation in his notepad.

Leaving the stoic and isolated farmer behind, Winston walked back to his car, the image of Gordon gazing over his desolate farm, framed by the town cemetery slowly fading away in the rearview mirror. His evening walk later would follow the usual path towards the cemetery. Gordon might be an immigrant here, but the cemetery and the isolation made him a local... and a person of interest.

Winston stood by the window in the chalet, gazing at the dense forest that surrounded the remote building. The last golden rays of the setting sun were piercing through the firs, illuminating the disturbingly peaceful crime scene where Harry met his end.

"Winston." His name was uttered by a bulky figure standing at the edge of the woods. He turned to see Dexter approaching him, his hulking silhouette cast in shadows by the setting sun.

"Evening." Winston greeted. "You're Dexter, right?"

"That's right." Dexter responded, a friendly smile replacing his creased frown. "I'm guessing you're here about Harry."

"We'll have to speak about that." Winston confessed. "Did you often hunt around these parts?"

Isaac, the ever-vigilant whistleblower, was preparing to expose Milton's scandalous scheme - a revelation that could land Milton in prison.

As Winston continued his investigation, his next stop was to meet with Max. Max ran a popular art dealership in town, claiming to deal with artifacts too, and his reputation had charmed many art enthusiasts, including Dwayne. 

Upon knocking, the door creaked open. Winston found himself in a large living space, filled with exquisite pieces of art, including a rather unique sickle, which was oddly intriguing.

"Max?" Winston called out, taking care not to disturb the artifacts around him.

Max returned from another room, a pleased grin on his face, his eyes kindling with pride," Ah, detective, welcome to my humble abode."

Max was a known art dealer who wasn't just after profit but cherished the art of curating a meaningful collection. From Winston's observation, Max appeared to be highly concerned about his reputation in this field.

When Winston asked, "Did Dwayne visit you last night?”, from the corner of his eye he noticed a flicker of unease cross Max’s face. Max hesitated before answering, "Yes, Detective. He wanted to take a look at my collection... he had a soft spot for historical farming artifacts."

As they chatted, Max admitted to giving Dwayne a ride afterward as Dwayne was his guest, and thought it only right to drive him back. Dwayne was seated in the passenger's seat of Max's car, he had said. It was in this same car where Dwayne's lifeless body was found later. 

"So it was just the two of you going to the car?", Winston clarified, to which Max nodded, confirming that he was last seen with Dwayne heading towards the car.

As the discussion continued, Winston learnt from Max about an upcoming exhibit, where Dwayne planned to expose an inauthentic artifact in Max's collection, something that threatened Max’s reputation.

On leaving, Winston couldn't help but echo the words of an old mentor. In a world where reputation is synonymous with one's identity, public humiliation would surely be a blow to anyone's individuality.

With that he exited, leaving a rather perturbed Max behind him, contemplating the implications.

Winston found himself standing in the midst of Anthony's gallery. The room was a silent symphony of colors and emotions, none of which were gold. But gold was the color he was concerning himself with today. Anthony's housekeeper had testified that she found gold paint on his clothes after his various trips, an unusual finding considering none of his displayed art contained any hint of the metallic hue.

He stepped out to speak with the gallery owner, his heavy boots echoing slightly in the hushed rooms. "He uses gold paint?" Winston asked, waving a test report he had from Anthony's housekeeper.

"No, not ever in his career. Anthony's palette is more primary," the gallery owner stated, looking rather puzzled.

After a short nod, Winston tucked away the paper, and left the gallery. His next stop in the long journey would be to confront Anthony himself. Anthony had earlier on requested a meeting with Dwayne. He decided to use this unusual request as leverage, he agreed now to meet Winston by Dwayne's car, a location he knew well since he had keys to it. He pulled out his phone to arrange this unusual meeting.

Anthony looked a bit out of place amongst the urban landscape, amongst the shining cars. His hair was a wild mane and colors smudged his skin artistically. A keychain, bulky and jingling with keys, sat by his side. 

"I had to pick up some of Dwayne's things", Anthony said, hand unconsciously stroking the keychain. "His woman couldn’t do it, she's a wreck."

"You had keys to his car?" Winston prompted.

"Well, yes, we were friends after all," Anthony replied, confirming his synaptic tie to Dwayne's automobile. 

Winston decided to take a different approach for the kind of question that lay heavy on his mind. "Dwayne didn't share your religious beliefs, did he?" He said, more of a statement than a question.

Anthony's face twisted, his features hardened. "No, he didn't, the fool was way off the path. He never got my art, my sermons. I've often stated in my preachings that the nonbelievers like him were threatening the sanctity of our path."

Anthony looked uncomfortable when he realized what he had just said, and he tried to compose himself. "He needed help, that’s why I wanted to meet him. Sure, I was deeply offended by his criticism, but that doesn't make my concern any less valid."

"To convince him about your beliefs?" Winston posed, a touch of humanity in his tone.

"No, to make him understand my art!" Anthony's voice was emphatic. But he didn’t admit to painting with gold.

"There were disagreements then?" Winston asked, almost rhetorically.

A deep sigh rasped out from Anthony's mouth. "Yes, often. Unfortunately, I was unable to win him over."

He looked down at his hands, the same hands that relentlessly splashed beautiful, and often disturbing, illusions onto canvas. And then a grim realization reflected on his face, a bitter parting comment reminding him of the deep offense Dwayne’s criticism might have caused. The open space around Dwayne's car echoed with the ringing silence-the paradoxical sound of an artist remorseful.

"Ah, it doesn’t matter now." Anthony got up to leave, a sad brush of reality tinted his voice.

The man was an artist, devoted to his spiritual path to the point of obsession. But enough to commit a murder? Winston wondered, the many pieces of this puzzle yet to find their right place.<turn|>

In the heart of a lively soccer field, Ivy succumbs to a fatal poisoned drink, leaving suspects Meredith and Hugo to face the relentless inquiries of Detective Winston.

Winston walked his fingers over the glossy crime scene photos spread out before him. The soccer field, typically a place of good-hearted competition and family fun, had been turned into a spectacle of horror as Ivy met her untimely end. The only saving grace was that the game had been called off before the tragedy unfolded.

Ivy was a frequent attendee of these games, often seen happily sipping on a cold drink from the stand. This time, it had been her undoing.

Winston was no rookie, but cases like these sent a cold shiver up his spine. Putting the photos back into the case file, it was time to pay Hugo a visit. 

Hugo was perched on a stool in the recording booth when Winston arrived. Despite the match being called off, Hugo had been working as a sound engineer at the same match. His work as a sound engineer was only a few blocks away from the matchplex, it was a stone throw away. Working with sound engineering also meant that Hugo had to handle chemicals regularly as part of his job role. Winston noticed a tattoo peeking from the arms of Hugo's rolled-up flannel – the name Anna, inked with what seemed like a real sense of devotion.

"Hugo?" Winston asked, leaning against the doorframe.

"That's me," Hugo replied, his eyes never leaving the windows of his booth.

"I hear you were serving refreshments at the match yesterday," Winston said, trying to keep his tone neutral.

"I was, yeah," Hugo confirmed with a nod, "I often help out there."

"You've been seen leaving work that day, "Winston continued.

"Yeah, I left to go set up the refreshments," Hugo responded.

At first glance, Hugo didn’t seem like the type who would care about a toxicology course, but records indicated he had taken one in the past. Moreover, his work required him to handle complex sound equipment which could involve frequent contact with certain chemicals.

Winston circled back to Hugo's protective side. "You seem close to Anna."

"Yeah," Hugo’s gaze softened, "hee, she's like my baby sister. I've always looked out for her."

Any detective worth his salt knew how protective bonds could drive people to extreme lengths. Winston had heard from others about some cruel remarks Ivy made about ruining Anna and of threats to press charges against her. 

"All right Hugo," Winston said, throwing his coat over his arm, "thank you for your time."

Winston had more pieces to the puzzle now, but he knew the killer wouldn't reveal himself easily. Winston, as always, would be waiting patiently. After all, a game of cat and mouse was half the thrill of his job.

Winston's latest case had piqued his curiosity, leading him to a popular coffee shop downtown where Ivy, the person of interest, was a regular. As he strolled in, the distinct aroma of dark roasted beans permeated the air. Behind the counter, Meredith worked with great efficiency amidst the morning rush. 

"Ivy was a regular here?" Winston questioned and Meredith nodded. "Every morning, like clockwork. Black coffee, a splash of half-and-half. No sugar,” she described Ivy's drink preference.

From a nearby television, a clip replayed on the local news – Ivy, laughing boister⟦ously⟧ whilst imitating some sacred rituals, unmistakenly disrespecting Meredith's beliefs. Winston looked towards Meredith, who now busied herself with a new order – an infusion of a variety of substances readily on hand: chocolate shavings, cinnamon sprinkles, and an endless assortment of flavored syrups.

"Do you mix all the drinks?" Winston asked. Meredith, too preoccupied, responded with a nod. Every shift, Winston noted, Meredith would arrive donning religious symbols around her neck. Today was no exception. As she prepared for her work day, her fingers grazed her amulets and she muttered a silent prayer before diving into the morning pandemonium.

Meredith often spoke publicly about being a staunch follower of her religion and openly declared – more times than Winston would care to count – that anyone who disrespects her beliefs deserves severe punishment.

Right when the morning rush started to wear off, Meredith slipped into the backroom, tugging off her apron. Winston’s eyes landed on a bag near the entrance - a familiar logo from the local butcher shop from where she regularly purchased raw meat.

In the midst of the bustling shop, Winston's attention was drawn to a framed photograph. Meredith was captured mid-spit, a chicken wing in hand.

"But she only buys raw meat," the butcher's words echoed in his mind, contrary to the image he was witnessing. He recalled Meredith’s friends' words: "Meredith has never had cooked meat in front of us."

With lunchtime approaching, the crowd began to ebb and Winston found a moment to delve deeper. In a passing query, he asked, "Heard about the news? Ivy, laughing at your beliefs - that was caught on camera."

Meredith’s hands clenched a coffee cup so tightly it overflowed. In her eyes burned recognition and some suppressed pain. She merely muttered how disrespectful Ivy was.

A customer chimed in, ordering a highly customized drink and Winston’s observation heightened as he watched Meredith expertly mask all traces of the various ingredients she used in the drink. A craft eerily similar to certain practices of subterfuge.

As Winston reached out to accept his coffee—an all-black with a splash of half and half, he pondered over the peculiar pieces of the jig-saw. His goodbye was met with a cautionary note from Meredith, "Hey detective, respect every belief you come across... seems like the world could use more of that, you know?”

As Winston stepped onto the sidewalk, Meredith’s words left him with a chilling twist in his investigation.<turn|>

The crowbar didn't seem out of place, what with her being a metal worker and competitively acknowledged for her unique metalwork.

Her performance at work had been nothing short of outstanding, and she had been putting in long, overtime hours. She was highly dedicated to her work and never missed an opportunity to express her ambition for a promotion.

Julian and Clara both worked at the same company, and both had been in the running for the same promotion. During the office water cooler chats, he'd heard Clara express her keen interest in the promotion, and her evident disappointment when Julian became a potential contender.

The evidence was laid in front of him: a woman with an enthusiastic interest in killers,⟦ always⟧ reading her crime books even on her lunch breaks, a craftsman with a signature touch on uniquely crafted crowbars, and seen with one on the day of Julian's infamous dive. A metal worker who had been putting in long hours for an impressive performance. All that tied with the delicate balance of coworkers both competing for the same promotion. 

One piece of evidence caught his eye. Clara was also a part of the diving team on the day Julian was murdered. With that, Winston pushed back his chair, stood up, and prepared to pay Clara a visit. He had a feeling there would be more to dig up from her perpetually stacked workspace, files and statements during her interrogation.

She'd even taken a boat maintenance course somewhere along the way. A crowbar tool was commonly used in both professions.

"Justin," Winston called out, making his way over. As soon as Justin heard the detective's approach and caught sight of the man in uniform, his eyes instantly lit up, always eager to gain more information about the crime.

"Detective," Justin greeted, his expression somber, yet subtly eager, "here for the game or here about the recent crime?"

Winston raised a brow. Justin seemed too interested. "Any hockey fan would be here for the game," he replied, "Marvin was going to play, wasn't he?"

Justin's dry eyes took on a spark when the murder was mentioned again. He looked dejected at the mention of Marvin, but nodded, "Yeah, he was. I was here to watch it." He had been with the crowd entering the hockey rink at the time of the murder, ready for the game and totally unprepared for the tragedy that eventually unfolded.

He paused, glancing around the rink, then asked, "Do you know how they got in? The murderer, I mean."

Winston kept his expression unreadable, but he noted Justin's quick change of topic back to the crime. "Through the main entrance," he stated simply, "like anyone else," he added, reaffirming that Justin had entered the same way.

"And the time... when exactly did it happen?" Justin changed the topic right back to the crime again, the flame in his eyes burning brighter at the prospect of new details.

Winston frowned slightly, "During the game," he answered, watching Justin's face carefully. He appeared unphased.

Justin cocked a brow, excitement mixed with intrigue evident in his lit eyes. "I was here during that time," he pointed out, "Watching the game."

Winston nodded, "You were, and as far as anyone knows, you didn't leave until well after," he almost sighed, "Listen Justin, what exactly is it with you and this crime? It seems that you're more interested in it than the hockey game."

Justin shifted, looking anywhere but at him, "Well, it's just...Marvin and his fiancé, you know. I just thought they...weren't right for each other. I had a talk with her once. I asked her not to marry him. But she didn't listen."

In the wake of Lola's mysterious katana-driven demise at a secluded mountain cabin, Detective Winston finds himself entangled in a web of suspicion, with Isabelle and Frank peering anxiously from its corners.

In the tempered light of the police station, Detective Winston flipped open the file for his latest case. Pinned to the top was a grim photo of Lola, the victim, marking another life prematurely ended. A set of intimate text messages from Lola to another man caught his attention, reportedly found by Isabelle. Winston found the content of the messages interesting, adding more intrigue to the case. Lower in the pile, there was a picture of Isabelle, his prime suspect. 

With a dedication observed during her thrice weekly visits, Isabelle had become a familiar figure in her local dojo, her commitment noted by fellow practitioners. Winston dialed the dojo and had a brief but informative conversation with her sensei, before putting the phone back with a small sigh. Her sensei revealed that Isabelle had been seen sharpening her Katanas after each session.

David, Lola's life coach, had confided a lot in Isabelle, spending a considerable amount of time alone with her, a fact that Winston found odd. Isabelle had not only found some of Lola's intimate messages, but she had also seen Lola kissing the unknown man, making her knowledge even more suspect. The phone buzzed back into life, David at the other end of the line filling Winston in on his last intimate conversation with Isabelle. Their relationship was unconventional - it didn’t seem standard for a life coach to be so close to a friend of their clients.

“What brings you up here, Detective?” Isabelle asked when Winston arrived at her door. She was out of breath and had chalk dusted on her pants, evident either from her routine rock climbing training or her regular hike which she often indulged in.

Winston followed Isabelle into the house and entered a room solely dedicated to her Katana collection. Some were ornate, clearly for show, but others showed signs of recent care, with the wear marks from constant sharpening along the blade, the same the sensei had mentioned.

“So, you visit Lola’s mountain cabin often?” Winston asked, shifting the conversation. 

“Yeah, I’ve been up there a handful of times when Lola is alone. It’s quiet and at a considerable altitude, inaccessible without physical fitness, perfect to clear the mind,” Isabelle admitted. She described the layout of the cabin in detail, showing her familiarity with the place. But her voice seemed somewhat strained, the memory of seeing Lola and the man in an intimate exchange casting a shadow.

They talked a while longer about the trails to the cabin, which Winston rightly noted required considerable physical strength. The conversation then swung to David, and they spoke freely about their close, somewhat unconventional friendship.

Upon his return to the dojo, Winston observed the elegance and precision with which the sensei moved a katana. His mind drifted back to the crime scene, Lola’s body lying in an eerily tranquil way, as if her death had been executed by someone trained in a lethal art. 

Back in the car, Winston flicked his cigarette butt into the darkness, a chill passing over him as he thought of Lola, alone in the cabin at the time she was killed. What a dark sense of humor life had, he reflected, as he prepared to tackle the case.

As Winston paced the floor of his small and cluttered office, he reviewed his notes about Lola's murder. The whole scene of the gruesome act was set in a secluded mountain cabin, salted wounds for the peaceful surroundings. She had invited Frank for a work retreat, a secret invitation that he told no one about, and Winston decided that perhaps it was time to visit the suspect.

As a biologist, Frank was surrounded by microscopes and lab coats by the day, while his nights were spent in a dojo, practicing martial arts. Winston's curiosity piqued upon learning of his weapon of choice, the katana. 

Winston carefully examined Frank's martial arts record and noticed Frank's regularity in practicing with his katanas. A clue that Winston found interesting was the fact that Frank recently acquired a sharpening stone. An unusual purchase when you considered his profession.

Frank's laboratory colleagues had divulged that he often had a peculiar habit. He would abruptly leave work and colleagues found new insect bites on his skin afterwards. This could be nothing⟦ more⟧ than a biologist exploring his environment, but Winston had a gut feeling that there was more to it.

Winston had also come across Frank's bank statements, where funds were frequently withdrawn to flight booking sites. Odd for someone whose work seemed to revolve mostly around his lab, but not out of the ordinary either.

Frank's home had companion pets who were frequently ill during his unexplained absences. Curiously, this seemed to coincide with his unusual hobby of abruptly leaving his office and heading in the unknown, Winston made a mental note to investigate Frank's suspicious departures more closely.

On the day of Lola's murder, Frank's schedule had no entries. Couple that with an eye-witness account of him being seen near the mountain cabin and Winston decided it was time to reach out to this elusive biologist. As he dialed Frank's number, Winston knew that he was getting closer to unveiling the truth. "Mr. Frank," he said, "It's Detective Winston, let's talk."<turn|>
